title: Moral certainty from constant fame and common consent
source_text: IX. Denique est certitudo quaedam quam fama constans ingenerat, & consensus hominum tam confirmatus & celebris, ut a mente prorsus excludat omnem formidinem & dubitationem. Ita nemo est, cui sit aliquis rerum & literarum usus, qui non indubitate & certissime sibi persuadeat populum Romanum olim Consules suos habuisse: & postea fuisse Imperatoribus subjectum. Item esse in Thracia urbem nomine Constantinopolim, quae sedes est magni cujusdam imperii: & Hispaniae regem Americae partem maximam subegisse, & illi dominari. Ista vero postrema certitudinis species, ut & illa de qua Thesi superiori, in Scholis certitudo Moralis appellari solet.
pass_a_gloss: Finally there is a certain certainty which constant fame generates, and a consensus of men so confirmed and celebrated that it altogether excludes from the mind every fear and doubt. So there is no one who has any use of affairs and letters who does not indubitably and most certainly persuade himself that the Roman people once had their Consuls, and afterward were subject to Emperors; likewise that there is in Thrace a city named Constantinople, which is the seat of a certain great empire; and that the king of Spain has subdued the greater part of America and rules it. But this last species of certainty, as also that of which in the Thesis above, is wont to be called in the Schools moral certainty.
pass_b_english: Certainty from constant fame + celebrated human consensus.
Excludes fear and doubt (Rome’s consuls/emperors; Constantinople; Spain in America).
With VIII’s sign-certainty: Schools call this certitudo Moralis.
